newsitem.title: UK: British rates seen staying put as election looms.
newsitem.headline: British rates seen staying put as election looms.

text.p: British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England governor Eddie George were due to meet on Thursday afternoon but no change to interest rates was expected ahead of the May 1 election.
The meeting, which will start at 1415 GMT (1515 BST), will be in Nottingham, Central England instead of the normal venue of London, because of the Chancellor's campaign commitments.

Analysts say the proximity of the vote, which is expected to result in the ousting of Clarke's ruling Conservative Party, virtually rules out a rise in Britain's 6.0 percent official rate despite signs the economy is growing too quickly.
"The chance of a rate rise today is as close to zero as any event could conceivably be," said Yamaichi chief economist John Shepperd.
"It just seems inconceivable given all the circumstances and politics surrounding the meeting," he said.

The Conservatives are around 20 points behind the opposition Labour party and analysts doubt Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke would want to risk antagonising voters by raising interest rates this close to polling day.

George is expected to reiterate his recent calls -- which have been rejected -- for a 1/4 point increase in interest rates to dampen demand in the vibrant consumer sector even though he has little hope of success.
"Governor George is privately resigned to continued differences with Mr Clarke over the appropriate monetary stance," said UBS economist Alex Garrard.
"He will simply be rehearsing the arguments that in the coming months he will put before a new audience, one which is likely to prove more receptive to his policy demands," he said.
If Labour wins the May election, then Gordon Brown is expected to be appointed chancellor and is likely to agree to the Bank's request for a tighter monetary policy stance.
"A Labour chancellor will do whatever the Bank wants and can blame it on the previous government," Royal Bank of Scotland economist Marian Bell said.

After 18 years in opposition, Labour is desperate to show that it is not the same party which allowed inflation, borrowing and spending to soar in the 1970s and a prompt interest rate rise would help establish credibility with financial markets.
The next monetary meeting is provisionally set for May 7, giving Brown an early opportunity to establish anti-inflation credentials.
"We could get two 1/4 point rises fairly rapidly," Yamaichi's Shepperd said. "But 6.5 percent might well be the top of the cycle for interest rates," he said.
But if Labour takes a rise in interest rates is unlikely to be the only change to monetary policy.
The party has pledged to overhaul the whole framework, which it says is too personalised and too vulnerable to political manipulation.

Instead of the current monthly meetings between the Chancellor and the central bank governor, the meeting will be with a new monetary policy committee, made up of representatives of the central bank, including the governor, and three or four outsiders.

The current panel of independent forecasters who offer advice to the Treasury on the economy will be replaced by a new Council of economic advisers and the dates of monetary meetings will be announced some months in advance.
But the reforms stop short of making the Bank of England independent and as such still leave interest rate decisions up to the Chancellor who is, after all, a politician.
"The proposals should be viewed as a step towards greater independence for the bank but for the time being the political slant of policy working will remain absolutely in place," UBS's Garrard said.
